name: Equal-Subset-Sum and Pigeonhole Equal Subset Sum
description: Two closely related subset-balancing variants whose exponential target of O*(2^{n/3}) has already been reached for the pigeonhole case, while the unrestricted case still lags far behind. Equal-Subset-Sum (ESS): given n integers w_1,...,w_n with |w_i| <= 2^{poly(n)}, find two distinct subsets A, B with sum_{i in A} w_i = sum_{i in B} w_i. Pigeonhole Equal Subset Sum (PESS, Papadimitriou 1994): given n positive integers with total sum < 2^n - 1, find two distinct subsets with equal sum; a solution is guaranteed by the pigeonhole principle, so PESS is a total-search problem in the class PPP. The known exponential records are: PESS solved by a randomized algorithm in O*(2^{n/3}) (Stan Zhang, MIT Master's thesis 2024; refined by Ce Jin, Ryan Williams, Stan Zhang, ESA 2025), improving Jin and Wu's O*(2^{0.4n}) (ICALP 2024) and the O*(2^{n/2}) meet-in-the-middle baseline. For unrestricted ESS the best worst-case time is O*(1.6994^n) (Yamano-Shibuya 2026), improving O*(1.7067^n) (Randolph-Wegrzycki, STOC 2026) and O*(1.7088^n) (Mucha-Nederlof-Pawlewicz-Wegrzycki, ESA 2019). A recent FOCS 2026 paper (Bhati-Dutta-Joux-Rajasree-Wegrzycki) gives a deterministic poly(n)*M^{o(1)} pseudopolynomial algorithm for dense PESS (M = 2^{o(n)}), an average-case poly(n)*M^{1/4} algorithm, and a conditional lower bound tying substantially faster PESS algorithms to breakthroughs on approximate lattice problems (including finding short lattice vectors). For vanilla Subset Sum, by contrast, O*(2^{n/3}) remains far out of reach and even an O(2^{(1/2-eps)n}) worst-case algorithm is open.
worst_case_time: PESS: O*(2^{n/3}) time by a randomized algorithm (Jin-Williams-Zhang, ESA 2025; originally Zhang's MIT Master's thesis 2024), a polynomial-space variant in O*(2^{2n/3}) time and poly(n) space (same paper). Prior state of the art O*(2^{0.4n}) randomized (Jin-Wu, ICALP 2024) and O*(2^{n/2}) via meet-in-the-middle or mod-p DP (Allcock-Hamoudi-Joux-Klingelhofer-Santha, ESA 2022). Dense pseudopolynomial regime: deterministic poly(n)*M^{o(1)} when M = 2^{o(n)}, and average-case poly(n)*M^{1/4} (Bhati-Dutta-Joux-Rajasree-Wegrzycki, FOCS 2026), improving the prior poly(n)*M^{1/3}. Unrestricted ESS: O*(1.6994^n) time (Yamano-Shibuya, arXiv 2026), improving O*(1.7067^n) (Randolph-Wegrzycki, STOC 2026) and O*(1.7088^n) (MNPW, ESA 2019); the meet-in-the-middle baseline is O*(3^{n/2}) = O*(1.7321^n). A 2026 single-author preprint claims a one-sided Monte Carlo ESS algorithm in O((5/3)^n) = O(1.6667^n) time [unrefereed].
space_complexity: PESS: O*(2^{n/3})-time algorithm uses exponential space; an explicit time-space point is O*(2^{2n/3}) time with poly(n) space (Jin-Williams-Zhang, ESA 2025). Unrestricted ESS: the O*(1.6994^n)-time algorithm of Yamano-Shibuya uses O*(1.5664^n) space; polynomial-space ESS runs in O*(2.5430^n) time (improving O*(2.6817^n) of MNPW 2019). Other exact space exponents are not specified here.
model: Classical word RAM / unit-cost RAM (integer inputs of |w_i| <= 2^{poly(n)}). PESS is additionally studied as a TFNP total-search problem and is conjectured PPP-complete (Papadimitriou 1994); it is not a quantum result.
randomized_or_deterministic: Mixed by result. PESS O*(2^{n/3}) and O*(2^{2n/3}) are randomized (Monte Carlo, succeeded up to poly(n) factors); Jin-Wu O*(2^{0.4n}) is randomized. The FOCS 2026 dense M = 2^{o(n)} algorithm is deterministic; its poly(n)*M^{1/4} algorithm is randomized and holds in the average case. Unrestricted ESS algorithms (MNPW, Randolph-Wegrzycki, Yamano-Shibuya) are randomized/one-sided; the original MNPW 2019 result is randomized as well.
time_space_tradeoff_curve: Partial. For PESS a polynomial-space point is O*(2^{2n/3}) time / poly(n) space versus O*(2^{n/3}) time / exponential space. For unrestricted ESS, Yamano-Shibuya (2026) investigate time-space tradeoffs and improve running times across a broad range of exponential-space budgets; the extremes are O*(1.6994^n) time with O*(1.5664^n) space and O*(2.5430^n) time with polynomial space. No single closed-form family is stated in the sources consulted.
numerical_exponent_and_record_year: PESS exponential exponent 1/3 (base 2, about 0.3333n), attained 2024 (Zhang's thesis) and refined/published 2025 (Jin-Williams-Zhang, ESA 2025); previous record exponent 0.4 (Jin-Wu, ICALP 2024), against the 0.5 meet-in-the-middle baseline. Unrestricted ESS base 1.6994 (2026), down from 1.7067 (2026) and 1.7088 (2019). Dense PESS pseudopolynomial record M^{1/4} average-case and M^{o(1)} deterministic in the M = 2^{o(n)} regime (FOCS 2026).
problem_variant: Equal-Subset-Sum (ESS) and its pigeonhole-promised special case PESS. Both are Subset Balancing instances with coefficient set C = {-1,0,1} and target 0 (assign c_i in {-1,0,1}, not all zero, with sum c_i w_i = 0). Related to Partition (C = {-1,1}) and to the total-search class PPP.
applies_to: ESS: n integers w_1,...,w_n with |w_i| <= 2^{poly(n)}, find distinct A, B with equal sum (if one exists). PESS: n positive integers w_1 < ... < w_n with total sum < 2^n - 1, find distinct A, B with equal sum (always exists). The pseudopolynomial FOCS 2026 results are stated for PESS with weights bounded by M in the dense regime M = 2^{o(n)} and in the average case.
coefficient_set: C = {-1,0,1} for ESS/PESS (|C| = 3); PESS additionally restricts to positive weights and the promise sum w_i < 2^n - 1. It is the 'symmetric' family [-1:1] of Subset Balancing, as opposed to Subset Sum / Partition with C = {0,1} or {-1,1}.
density_regime: PESS spans all densities but has a distinguished dense/pseudopolynomial regime: with M = max w_i, density d = n/log2 M. When M = 2^{o(n)} (high density, small bit-length) the FOCS 2026 algorithm runs deterministically in poly(n)*M^{o(1)} = 2^{o(n)} time; the average-case bound is poly(n)*M^{1/4}, improving poly(n)*M^{1/3}. The exponential O*(2^{n/3}) result is density-agnostic under the pigeonhole promise.
solution_regime: ESS is general decision/search (a solution may not exist); PESS is a promised many-solution / total-search regime where a solution is guaranteed by pigeonhole and the goal is only to find one (PPP total search).
cardinality_constraint: No fixed-cardinality constraint is imposed; solutions A, B may have any sizes (and can be assumed disjoint since (A\B, B\A) preserves equality).
key_technique: PESS (Jin-Wu -> Jin-Williams-Zhang): a structural characterization via F = sum_t max(0, f_t - 1), the number of colliding subset-sum pairs. If F is small the input must be close to the geometric progression 1,2,4,...,2^{n-1} up to additive error F; this bounds |w_i - 2^{i-1}| and forces every solution to come from a poly(n)-sized set of 'close pairs' X,Y of high-index elements, reducing the task to a much smaller Equal Subset Sum instance on the low k+1 elements with large F; if F is large, subsampling hits a solution and mod-p dynamic programming solves it. Jin-Williams-Zhang exploit the structural property even in the many-solution case, reducing to a small number of smaller ESS instances and balancing to 2^{n/3}. FOCS 2026 (Bhati-Dutta-Joux-Rajasree-Wegrzycki) uses block merging and modular pruning for the deterministic dense M = 2^{o(n)} algorithm, a birthday-paradox-based algorithm for the weak-pigeonhole regime, and Karmarkar-Karp differencing, plus an average-case analysis.
core_idea: The number of equal-sum pairs F measures how far the input is from the worst-case geometric progression. Small F means the numbers are nearly 1,2,4,...,2^{n-1}, so any equal-sum relation is tightly constrained and involves few 'close' high-order choices; this collapses PESS to a tiny ESS instance. Large F means solutions are abundant, so random subsampling and mod-p subset-sum counting find one quickly. Jin and Wu used the small-F structure but handled large F by subsampling; Jin-Williams-Zhang reused the structure in the large-F case to shrink the effective instance size, which is what buys the clean 2^{n/3} exponent. The FOCS 2026 line instead works in the pseudopolynomial parameter M and shows the M^{1/4} barrier is essentially tight under lattice hardness.
reduction_pipeline: PESS -> smaller Equal Subset Sum: guess poly(n) many 'close pairs' (X,Y) of elements outside the low block [k] (with k ~ log2 F), then solve an Equal Subset Sum instance on k+1 integers with large F via subsampling + mod-p dynamic programming (Jin-Wu Lemma 5/6). The FOCS 2026 conditional lower bound goes the other direction, reducing (approximate) lattice problems to fast PESS algorithms, i.e. a fast PESS algorithm would yield a breakthrough for finding short lattice vectors.
constructive_vs_existential: Constructive: the algorithms return an explicit pair of distinct subsets A, B with equal sum. PESS guarantees existence, and the algorithms produce the witness.
search_vs_decision_witness: Search/witness: PESS and ESS algorithms return the actual two subsets; PESS never returns a false witness. Constructivity is proved for the randomized PESS algorithm (success probability 1 - o(1) after amplification).
obstacle_to_2n3: For PESS the 2^{n/3} target is already attained but not beaten; the exponential algorithm is not known to be optimal and going below 2^{n/3} is open. The FOCS 2026 lattice-based conditional lower bound indicates that large further improvements in the pseudopolynomial parameter would imply breakthroughs on approximate lattice problems, so progress is expected to be constrained unless lattice hardness is circumvented. For unrestricted ESS the gap is much larger: the best worst case is around 1.6994^n (exponent ~0.7664 in base 2), so the 2^{n/3} target is not attained at all; the ESS techniques (representation method, bounded-space tradeoffs) do not obviously transfer to vanilla Subset Sum or reach 2^{n/3}.
potential_to_break_mitm: High for PESS (meet-in-the-middle already broken: 2^{n/2} -> 2^{0.4n} -> 2^{n/3}) and high for unrestricted ESS (1.7321^n MITM beaten to 1.6994^n). Low/medium as a route to vanilla Subset Sum: the structural pigeonhole promise and the {-1,0,1} coefficient set are used essentially, and no transfer to C = {0,1} or C = {-1,1} is known.
barrier_evidence: Conditional lower bound: a substantially faster PESS algorithm would give a breakthrough for approximate lattice problems, including finding short lattice vectors (Bhati-Dutta-Joux-Rajasree-Wegrzycki, FOCS 2026) [precise GapSVP/SVP formulation and threshold not available in the consulted sources]. Papadimitriou (1994) conjectured PESS is PPP-complete, which would rule out a polynomial-time algorithm. The best prior pseudopolynomial bound poly(n)*M^{1/3} (Jin-Wu / Jin-Williams-Zhang) is improved to poly(n)*M^{1/4} in the average case, with the lower bound described as 'tight'. For ESS there is no matching conditional lower bound beyond the generic ETH/SETH statements for Subset Sum.
open_questions: Can PESS be solved faster than O*(2^{n/3}) (e.g. O*(2^{0.3n}) or better) and can the O*(2^{n/3}) algorithm be derandomized? What is the exact lattice assumption, reduction, and running-time threshold of the FOCS 2026 conditional lower bound, and does it extend to the exponential regime? Can the PESS structural technique (near-geometric input structure) or the block-merging/modular-pruning method be applied to unrestricted Equal-Subset-Sum, Partition, or vanilla Subset Sum? Can the poly(n)*M^{1/4} average-case bound be made worst-case, or proven tight unconditionally? Is the claimed O((5/3)^n) Monte Carlo ESS algorithm correct (it would supersede the currently cited state of the art if verified)?
conditional_hypothesis: Lattice hardness (hardness of approximating shortest-vector problems / finding short lattice vectors) underlies the FOCS 2026 PESS conditional lower bound; PPP-completeness of PESS (Papadimitriou 1994) underlies the belief that no polynomial-time algorithm exists; SETH gives conditional lower bounds in the pseudopolynomial regime for Subset Sum (Abboud-Bringmann-Hermelin-Shabtay). The O*(2^{n/3}) upper bound for PESS is unconditional (randomized).
worst_case_vs_average_case_guarantee: PESS O*(2^{n/3}) and the unrestricted-ESS algorithms are worst-case bounds (with internal randomness, one-sided error). The poly(n)*M^{1/4} FOCS 2026 result is explicitly average-case; the deterministic poly(n)*M^{o(1)} result holds worst-case but only for the dense regime M = 2^{o(n)}. The lattice conditional lower bound constrains algorithms in the average/pseudopolynomial regime.
cryptographic_regime: Relevant via the conditional lower bound connecting fast PESS to approximate lattice problems / finding short lattice vectors (FOCS 2026), linking the problem to the hardness assumptions underlying lattice-based cryptography. ESS and Subset Balancing are also connected to knapsack cryptanalysis through the representation technique, but the exponential algorithms here are worst-case and not direct attacks; no density/sample-key parameters are specified.
pseudopolynomial_interaction: Central. The FOCS 2026 results are formulated in the pseudopolynomial parameter M = max w_i: deterministic poly(n)*M^{o(1)} when M = 2^{o(n)}, and average-case poly(n)*M^{1/4} (improving poly(n)*M^{1/3}). The PESS structural lemma (near-geometric progression) and mod-p dynamic programming are pseudopolynomial techniques, and the same Jin-Wu subsampling lemma works for general Equal Subset Sum (the pigeonhole promise is not used in that step). This contrasts sharply with vanilla Subset Sum, where SETH rules out O(W^{1-eps}) pseudo-polynomial algorithms.

empirical_evidence: None reported: these are worst-case/average-case theoretical analyses with proofs; no benchmark datasets or experiments are given.
implementation_artifact: none found (no reference code or repository accompanying the PESS/ESS algorithms).
verification_method: For PESS: verify the Jin-Wu structural lemma (F small implies |w_i - 2^{i-1}| bounded by F, i.e. near-geometric progression), reproduce the reduction from PESS to a smaller Equal Subset Sum instance via close pairs, and check the mod-p dynamic-programming and subsampling subroutines to confirm the O*(2^{n/3}) balance. For ESS: reproduce the representation/bounded-space constructions and the time-space tradeoff analysis of Yamano-Shibuya, and run against brute force on small n and random instances. For the FOCS 2026 lower bound: check the reduction from the stated approximate lattice problem to PESS and the exact parameter mapping.
